scenes.title: 두 번째 편의 질문과 앞 편의 결과
lines: The first episode constructed a rotation and used its inverse to undo an operation. This episode composes turns and calculates how to reach a target direction.

After observing changes in an assembly part’s orientation, we reverse the order of the same two rotations and compare their results. Then we find the difference between current and target orientations and check it by rotating a direction vector.
First, separate the part’s orientation from its position. Undoing orientation and retracing a path are different problems.

scenes.title: 네 게임에서 입력과 결과 비교
lines: Compare the placement of an assembly part with a model that calculates its orientation. Connect the current direction, the applied rotation and the resulting direction.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: The inverse cancels the original operation. Observe an assembly part’s orientation separately from its position, then undo only the rotation in our model.

scenes.title: 반대 회전과 되돌리는 과정
lines: Observe the two circular faces and the direction of the elongated body. In Space Engineers 2, this assembled part is moved into place.
Both position and orientation must match the attachment point. In our model, we will undo only the tilt that has already been applied.
The game camera also moves. We therefore define the exact axis and angle separately in the following model.
An inverse swaps the input and output of a stored rotation; it differs from riding backward or negating velocity.
Separating bank from travel shows why undoing orientation and undoing position are different questions.
Next we will diagram multiplication order and reference frames.

scenes.title: 반대 기울기에서 두 회전의 합성으로
lines: The inverse canceled the rotation. Now observe the model’s red front axis and blue up axis.
Tilt and facing change together. Can we add components to compose our two defined rotations?
We first verify dot and cross products with small numbers, then read the Hamilton product.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Having undone one rotation, we can now compose two. As multiplication combined planar turns, three-dimensional composition uses a product containing dot and cross products.

scenes.title: 내적과 외적은 각각 무엇을 묻는가?
lines: The composition formula uses dot and cross products. First distinguish two questions: alignment and the direction determined by their ordered pair.
A dot product multiplies corresponding components and adds them. The dot of (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) is zero, meaning the directions are perpendicular.
A cross product returns a vector perpendicular to both. With our right-handed convention, x cross y is +z, while y cross x is -z.
That order dependence remains in rotation composition. We will read the scalar and vector parts of the Hamilton product separately.

scenes.title: 내적과 외적으로 곱셈 읽기
lines: Consider the Hamilton product written in scalar-vector form.
Its scalar is the scalar product minus the vector dot product.
Its vector sums the two scalar-vector products and the vector cross product.
Reversing the cross product changes its sign, exposing the usual noncommutativity.
Products are associative, so parentheses can move without permitting arbitrary order changes.
Some rotations, such as those about one axis, do commute. Check the actual operation and convention.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Reversing a cross product changed its result. We will now reverse the order of two axis rotations from the same initial direction and inspect the resulting orientations.

scenes.title: 적용 순서와 곱셈의 좌우
lines: We use the Hamilton convention in which a vector rotates as q times v times inverse q.
Applying fixed x90 followed by fixed y90 puts the y quaternion on the left.
The initial z direction becomes minus y after x90 and remains there under y90.
In reverse order it becomes x after y90 and remains x under x90, so the results differ.
A world-frame delta premultiplies the current orientation; a body-frame delta postmultiplies it.
Check whether a library uses the same product convention, using small axis-rotation probes.

scenes.title: 고정 축과 몸체 축을 분리해 관찰하기
lines: Changing rotation order changed the result. Compare the red axis attached to the model with the stationary reference lines.
Body axes turn with the object, while the world reference axes remain fixed.
Our calculation multiplied world-relative increments on the left and body-relative ones on the right.
How much further rotation takes the current orientation to a target?

scenes.title: 트레일메이커스: 물체의 방향과 보는 방향
lines: Observe the nose and wings of our computational airplane model. We keep its position fixed while changing its heading and tilt.
The camera and world reference axes also stay fixed. Reversing only the order of the same two rotations lets us directly compare the resulting difference.

scenes.title: 같은 두 회전의 순서를 바꾸기
lines: Start with the upward model direction zero, zero, one. A ninety-degree fixed-world x turn followed by a ninety-degree fixed-world y turn gives zero, minus one, zero.

Reversing the order gives one, zero, zero. The individual turns match, but the final directions differ. This connects our verified right-handed convention and product order to an aircraft orientation problem.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: The order of fixed-axis rotations changed the result. In the game, watch how turning the body also changes its attached directions; this motivates separating world and body frames.

scenes.title: 동작 순서와 기준을 관찰하기
lines: Use two copies of the same assembly part and change only the order of the applied rotations.
Turning the front direction also turns the body-relative axis used for the next rotation.
Follow temporal order; an endpoint frame does not reconstruct every intermediate operation.
Distinguishing fixed world axes from moving body axes is the starting point for choosing multiplication side.
Here, we define the model’s reference axes and order ourselves. These are not internal game rotations inferred from its screen image.
Observing the part’s front face and up axis together makes its complete orientation clearer than a single direction.

scenes.title: 현재 자세에서 목표 자세를 묻기
lines: The multiplication side determines the reference frame. Observe the red front axis separately from the object’s position.
Now define the current and target orientations directly in our model.
Call the current orientation a and the target b. Which additional rotation takes a to b?

scenes.title: 스페이스 엔지니어스: 현재 방향에서 목표 방향으로
lines: Turn the front face of the part toward the required direction: from its current orientation to its target orientation.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We have distinguished body and world frames. Now we can ask which extra rotation reaches a target orientation, and verify the answer by applying that delta.

scenes.title: 두 자세 사이의 회전 차이
lines: Let a be the current and b the target local-to-world orientation.
A world delta must satisfy delta times a equals b, so it is b times inverse a.
A body delta postmultiplies a, giving inverse a times b. Changing frames changes the order.
From z30 to z90, the same-axis difference is z60.
With mixed axes, component subtraction is insufficient. Use inverse and product, and name the reference frame.
Apply the computed delta back to the current orientation and verify that it reaches the target.

scenes.title: 같은 축에서 목표까지 남은 회전
lines: In the defined same-axis model, the current z rotation is thirty degrees and the target is ninety; the remaining rotation is sixty, not an additional ninety.

Applying the world difference D to the current orientation A yields target B: D A equals B. Thus D equals B times the inverse of A. This same-axis check does not justify subtracting angles across different axes.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We computed the required rotation difference. To determine how large it is, we will compare all four components and calculate the smallest angle between the final orientations.

scenes.title: 내적으로 최소 회전 각도 구하기
lines: The dot product sums products of all four quaternion components.
For the smallest physical relative rotation, take the absolute dot product.
Twice its arccos gives an angle from zero to 180 degrees.
Equivalent q and -q have dot minus one, whose absolute value gives zero rotation distance.
Validate unit inputs and clamp tiny numerical overshoot to [0,1] before arccos.
This measures minimal endpoint separation, not accumulated trick rotation or path direction.

scenes.title: 최소 자세 차이와 동작 전체의 길이
lines: The minimum angle compares two specified end orientations. Follow the model’s front and up axes.
Even if an object keeps rotating, one final orientation does not store all the intermediate motion.
Even a similar ending direction requires a time record to recover the intervening turn.
Compare two paths to the same final orientation side by side.
How do we construct an intermediate direction? Next, we calculate half of a rotation.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: The minimum angle compares end orientations. During assembly, distance to a target position and the difference from a target orientation are also separate quantities.

scenes.title: 목표 자세와 가까운 자세
lines: Specify the placement position separately from the direction the front face must point.
The required change depends on the target orientation you choose.
Orientation difference is separate from the remaining positional distance.
Similar-looking screen poses still require rotation data for exact angle computation.
Minimal angle describes nearest endpoint separation, not the full length of the actual motion.
Follow the part’s front face and up axis together. Separate where it should be placed from its orientation there.
We explicitly define two end orientations in this model. A direct turn and a different path can both reach the same target orientation.
An inverse or relative rotation that matches a pose does not rewind position or collisions. Motion path and rotational endpoint are separate records.
Imagine comparing stored current and target orientations; next we will apply a chosen fraction of a rotation.

scenes.title: 절반 회전은 네 숫자의 절반이 아니다
lines: Quaternion powers lead to scaling the rotation angle. Follow the model’s red front axis as its direction changes.
Keep position fixed and compare ninety degrees with half that angle about the same axis.
Halving an angle does not mean multiplying all four components by0.5.
Half of ninety degrees is forty-five. We verify the distinction with logarithms and exponentials.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We found the rotation to a target, but applying it all in one frame would produce an abrupt turn. We will first learn to apply a fraction of a fixed-axis rotation.

scenes.title: 회전의 절반과 숫자 크기의 절반
lines: We want to apply 45 degrees rather than all 90 degrees. Halving a turn is different from halving all four stored components.
Two 45-degree rotations about the same axis compose to 90 degrees. Our fractional rotation must satisfy that relationship.

A quaternion logarithm converts a chosen axis and half-angle into a convenient vector; its exponential converts that vector back to a unit quaternion. Start with these inverse roles rather than their names.
For z90, the log vector is the z axis times pi/4. Halving it gives a stored half-angle of 22.5 degrees and a physical turn of 45 degrees.
Different chosen axis-angle branches can share a final orientation yet have different intermediate paths. We must choose the path before taking fractional powers.

scenes.title: 회전의 일부를 적용하는 거듭제곱
lines: Given a chosen axis-angle representative, scale its angle while retaining its axis to form a fractional rotation.
Half of z90 is z45; this is not multiplication of all four components by 0.5.
A chosen logarithm stores the axis times half-angle as a pure quaternion, and the exponential reconstructs a unit quaternion.
Distinguish radians and the half-angle: the previous rotation vector used the full angle, whereas this logarithm uses half.
The power path depends on the selected sign and angle branch; fractional powers of q and -q can differ.
For a shortest path, choose the representative and boundary rules first, explicitly handling identity and half-turn ambiguity.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We can now construct a fractional rotation. To use it, we must apply it to a direction vector; let us check whether the single multiplication used in a plane still works in three dimensions.

scenes.title: 같은 벡터로 한쪽 곱과 양쪽 곱을 비교
lines: The initial complex example used one multiplication in a plane. To verify the earlier half-angle explanation, we return to the ninety-degree z-axis example. The input vector has x component one, y zero and z one.
To put a vector into the quaternion expression, prepend scalar zero. Define the letter C as square root of two divided by two. The rotation has scalar C, x and y zero, and z C.
The left multiplication alone produces scalar minus C and three vector components equal to C. Its nonzero scalar shows that this is not yet a three-dimensional direction vector.
Also multiply by the inverse on the right. That inverse has scalar C, x and y zero, and z minus C. The complete result has scalar zero, x zero, y one and z one.

Removing scalar zero leaves vector (0,1,1). The z component parallel to the rotation axis remains one while the original x component turns into y. The complete two-sided calculation verifies what the half-angle operation does.

scenes.title: 벡터는 왜 양쪽에서 곱할까?
lines: In the complex plane, multiplication by cos(angle)+i sin(angle) rotates a 2D vector.
In 3D, one-sided multiplication of a pure-vector quaternion generally creates a scalar and is not a vector rotation.
For v=(1,0,1), left multiplication by z90 alone creates scalar minus sqrt(2)/2.
Including the inverse on the right restores scalar zero and gives vector (0,1,1).
The axis-parallel z component remains, while x rotates into y.
Both-sided multiplication combines two half-angles into the physical angle; a worked vector makes the structure tangible.

scenes.title: 계산한 벡터를 물체에 붙여 읽기
lines: We checked the vector rotation. Observe the model’s red front axis and blue up axis together.
Distinguish the camera image from world-space orientation. Now read the calculated direction as one attached to the object.

scenes.title: 비시지: 계산 결과가 부품의 방향을 바꿉니다
lines: Observe the selected part’s front and up directions together. Interpret the calculated direction-vector change as a direction attached to the object.

scenes.title: 벡터 계산을 보이는 결과로 읽기
lines: Turning the model direction one, zero, one by ninety degrees around z gives zero, one, one. Its horizontal component changes while its vertical component remains one.

Both lengths are square root of two. Rotation changes direction and preserves length. This illustrates the effect of the sandwich product rather than estimating a real game’s angles or internal implementation.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: Our calculation turned x toward y while preserving the component parallel to the axis.
Now observe the directions attached to the object again.
We separate it from the camera frame that projects that direction on screen.

scenes.title: 카메라와 몸체가 함께 움직일 때
lines: Finally, keep the object fixed and move only the observing camera.
The front and side look different on screen, but the body axes stay fixed in the world. The camera provides another frame for displaying that state.
Separate making motion visible from computing orientation in world space.
With a stored quaternion, rotate direction vectors to obtain forward or up.
Pixels do not reveal the game storage format, but we can verify our defined mathematical example directly.
Now recheck component order and unit norm and solve the same calculation as an exercise.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We have connected stored components to a resulting direction. Reproducing that result in code requires matching the library's component order and coordinate conventions.

scenes.title: 코드에서 확인할 약속
lines: Four float32 components occupy sixteen bytes of component data, excluding alignment and metadata.
One more number than Euler angles can make composition and interpolation convenient, without guaranteeing superior speed for every use.
Euler angles may suit human editing, while precomputed matrices may suit rotating many directions.
Check storage order, Hamilton product, handedness, and the local-to-world convention together.
Maintain normalization and invalid-input guards, and distinguish component equality from orientation equality.
A quaternion represents rotation; it does not automatically solve collision, translation, or accumulated rotation history.

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: With the code conventions established, let us calculate the same input and result ourselves. Rotating and undoing it will verify that the formula restores the original vector.

scenes.title: 직접 돌리고 되돌려 보기
lines: First problem: rotate a vector ninety degrees about z. Its x is one, y is zero and z is one. What is the result? Pause and check the axes and signs.
Use [sqrt(2)/2,0,0,sqrt(2)/2] and the two-sided product on the pure vector.
The result is (0,1,1); x rotates into y and z remains. Length sqrt(2) is preserved.
Exercise two: should we negate all four components to restore the original vector?
No: use the unit conjugate, negating only the vector components. It restores (1,0,1).
Finally, decide whether an orientation difference is a world delta on the left or a body delta on the right.

scenes.title: 벡터의 결과에서 중간 자세의 질문으로
lines: We read orientation by rotating vectors. Now consider what lies between two orientations.
Observe the red front axis. How can we construct an intermediate orientation?

scenes.title: 다음 계산으로 연결하기
lines: We completed a rotation and its inverse. Using that result, let us return to our opening question: what do the four numbers store, and which operations do they support?

scenes.title: 네 숫자에서 회전 연산까지
lines: A quaternion has four components formed from a unit axis and half-angle, with three rotational degrees of freedom under its unit constraint.
q and -q represent one orientation; conjugation serves a different role, and the general inverse divides by squared norm.
Record product order and reference frames for composition and differences, then verify by applying the result.
Next we will interpolate orientations smoothly and safely convert among quaternion, matrix, Euler, and other representations.
